findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with datetime ordering
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then `int(math.floor(value) ... )`. When used with `order_by="-datetime"` (as the new audit-logs endpoint does), `value` is a `datetime` object, and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: float argument required, not datetime.datetime`. The existing DateTimePaginator has special handling (`float(value.strftime("%s.%f")) * self.multiplier`) for exactly this reason; OptimizedCursorPaginator is essentially a copy of `Paginator` (numeric-only) and is not a drop-in replacement for DateTimePaginator. The new `?optimized_pagination=true` path on the audit logs endpoint will 500 for any superuser/global-admin caller.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns raw timestamp instead of datetime
findings.body: value_from_cursor returns `cursor.value` directly. For datetime-keyed cursors that value is a Unix-timestamp integer produced by DateTimePaginator.get_item_key. The caller (BasePaginator.build_queryset) substitutes it into `WHERE <col> <= %s`, producing a comparison between a `datetime` column and an integer like `... WHERE datetime <= 1699999999000`, which PostgreSQL rejects with `operator does not exist: timestamp without time zone >= integer`. DateTimePaginator converts the integer back to a datetime; OptimizedCursorPaginator does not. Together with the get_item_key issue, the optimized audit-logs path is broken end-to-end.

findings.title: Negative-offset path is misleadingly documented and unsafe
findings.body: The `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0` branch claims in its comments that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', that it 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds', and that 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. None of these are true: Django translates `queryset[-N:M]` into `LIMIT (M-N) OFFSET -N`, which PostgreSQL rejects as a non-positive OFFSET, so the request 500s. The framing of 'efficient bidirectional pagination' misrepresents what negative slicing does — it returns the last N rows of the queryset, not an arbitrary position. The 'safe because permissions' justification conflates row-level authorization (which the queryset already enforces) with pagination-boundary integrity; allowing a client to choose a negative offset bypasses the `offset >= 0` invariant that BasePaginator and the rest of the pagination pipeline assume. The whole branch should be removed; it adds no legitimate functionality and exists only behind a parameter that is already gated to superusers, which makes the misleading comments more concerning.

findings.title: BasePaginator.get_result changes behavior for all subclasses, not just audit logs
findings.body: The diff replaces `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` with `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` and `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. This is a behavior change on a shared base class that affects every paginator inheriting from BasePaginator (DateTimePaginator, Paginator, MergingOffsetPaginator callers, etc.), not just the new OptimizedCursorPaginator. The PR title and description only mention audit logs and contain no mention of this base-class change, so reviewers of the other endpoints will not see it. The accompanying comment ('allow negative offsets to enable efficient bidirectional pagination') is the opposite of what the code does for non-prev cursors — it clamps negative offsets to 0, restricting rather than allowing them. This should either be reverted or split into its own PR with a real justification.

findings.title: Query-string flag exposes broken/unsafe paginator path to admins with no test coverage
findings.body: The new `?optimized_pagination=true` parameter routes the request through OptimizedCursorPaginator for any superuser or any member with global access. As noted above that paginator crashes on datetimes, mishandles cursor values, and contains the unsafe negative-offset branch. Gating behind `is_superuser or has_global_access` does not mitigate these issues; it just limits who sees the 500s. A security-relevant control surface (pagination of the audit log) is being routed through a new, untested code path with multiple bugs and a misleadingly-commented 'advanced' feature.

findings.title: No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or BasePaginator change
findings.body: The PR introduces a new paginator class with non-trivial behavior (enable_advanced_features flag, negative-offset branch, datetime-incompatible get_item_key/value_from_cursor) and modifies BasePaginator.get_result, but adds no tests. There are no tests covering: (1) the optimized audit-logs endpoint path, (2) pagination of datetime-ordered querysets through OptimizedCursorPaginator, (3) the negative-offset branch under enable_advanced_features, (4) the new max(0, offset) clamping in BasePaginator for non-prev cursors. Given that the new code is broken for datetime ordering, the lack of tests is what allowed the regressions to ship.

findings.title: cursors.py change is comment-only and the comment is misleading
findings.body: The diff adds two comment lines above `self.offset = int(offset)`. There is no code change — `int(offset)` was already there. The comment ('Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets') implies new functionality that was not actually added, and propagates the same misleading framing as the paginator changes. Either remove the comment or implement the documented behavior in a single place with a real test.
